messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] latent differential equation model, how to improve efficiency?
parts:
What transformation do you want? It sounds like you're just
building your own covariance matrix. If so, you just need to make
sure it's symmetric and positive definite.

> Without the automatic parameter transformations, I am not sure which prior
> to put on the X & dX covariance parameter XdX.
>
> Is there a better way to set up this model?

Not sure what you're trying to do. You'd want to put a prior on
the components you use to construct the covariance matrix, so you
don't need to declare anything a covariance matrix.

I'd recommend recoding that loop to only solve each covariance
matrix once and to simplify the index logic, which is too
error prone. Something like the following for J subjects:

FA[embedD + 3] = L3;
for (j in 1:J) {
FA[embedD + 1] = 1 + eta[j] * L3;
FA[embedD + 2] = L2 + zeta[j] * L3;
Sigma = quad_form_sym(S, FA);
X[start[j] : end[j]] ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
}

You add start[1:J] and end[1:J] for positions each
subject starts and ends in the X array. This will be much
faster because you only have to solve Sigma once.

I didn't trace through all the logic building a covariance matrix.

Direct scaling by hand might be faster than our quad form given that
you have a roughly diagonal matrix. All those multiplies by zero are
costly because they build out the expression graph.

- Bob

FA[embedD+1] = 1 + eta[px] * L3;
FA[embedD+2] = L2 + zeta[px] * L3;

Then I could add a prior for the correlation aspect,

stddev = sqrt(diagonal(Sigma));
for (cx in 1:embedD) {

cor ~ lkj_corr(1);

in the reply to me. If you construct a covariance matrix
yourself, you have to ensure it's positive definite. It's
a set of general quadratic equations, which I don't know how
to solve.

B. That won't work as you indicated yourself.

C. The only place I really have to ask around is this list!
